sections.html:
Hartford is Connecticut's capital, a river city in Hartford County with 121,054 people at the 2020 census living inside roughly 18 square miles. Vacant land is scarce. Lots are small, many buildings hold more than one unit, and buyers weigh one street against the next rather than treating the city as a single market.

The low ground along the Connecticut River has a flood record. In April 1909 the river reached 24.5 feet above low water and swamped part of the city, and it overflowed again in 1930. Anyone selling close to the water should be ready for basement and drainage questions. Hot, humid summers and snowy winters are also hard on roofs, gutters and furnaces, so a worn roof or a wet cellar is a common finding in an older house. Such houses still sell, because an as-is buyer simply subtracts the repair cost from the price.

The city splits the annual real estate bill into a July 1 installment and a January 1 installment. Each one carries a last day to pay, and when that day lands on a Saturday or Sunday it moves to the next Monday. The schedule appears on the Tax Collector's Tax Information page.

InstallmentDueLast day to pay
First installmentJuly 1August 1
Second installmentJanuary 1February 1

Once the last day has gone by, interest runs at 1.5% per month, a rate the city also expresses as 18% per year. Elderly owners whose applications are approved pay on a separate four-installment calendar: July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. It does not apply unless the city has approved your application.

sections.h2: Vehicle, personal property and abatement bills
sections.html:
Personal property and car tax run on the same July and January rhythm, with any bill above $100 divided into two payments. A car registered after October 2 receives a single supplemental bill due January 1.

Hardship relief goes through an abatement petition filed with the Tax Collector. It must be filled in completely, signed and notarized. The abatement committee gathers quarterly, and the city returns incomplete petitions without putting them on an agenda, so an error can cost you a whole quarter.

  • If you are about to register a vehicle, pay early. The DMV will not process the registration until the payment clears.
  • Cash, an in-person card or certified funds clear in about one business day, an online card in two, a check in ten.
  • Hold on to every receipt, because lost-receipt questions are on the office's own FAQ.

That same FAQ addresses recent buyers and sellers of Hartford houses who need to know what they owe. A phone call to the office gets you the number for your own parcel, and it is a better source than a general web search.

sections.h2: The Hartford closing: tax, deed and state form
sections.html:
At the table, the closing attorney or title company deducts unpaid property tax from your proceeds and then records the deed with the city. Since the tax year has two installments, a mid-year sale normally leaves one of them partly open, and your share of it shows up as a line on the settlement statement.

A state return travels with the deed. Form OP-236, the conveyance tax return, is submitted to the town clerk at recording by the grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent. It covers transfers of $2,000 or more unless an exemption applies, and the code for Hartford is 064. Instructions sit on the Department of Revenue Services conveyance tax page.

Owners in financial trouble should know about two exemptions. A principal residence handed over in lieu of foreclosure is exempt. So is a principal residence sold for less than the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and other lienable charges that rank ahead of them. Your closing attorney can tell you whether either describes your sale.

sections.h2: Questions for the Hartford tax office
sections.html:
An online account summary can trail a payment you made yesterday, and only the office can state the true balance on an account. When you call, work from this list:

  • What is owed as of today, with interest included?
  • Which installments show as paid, and when is the next one due?
  • Has a lien been recorded, and what must happen for a release?
  • Is the bill still going to a mortgage company, or does it come to you?

Request the answers in writing. With a written payoff in hand, the title company can fix a firm number for closing, and you will know what is left for you after the tax is cleared.

Here is the quickest route. First, gather your account number from the latest bill, along with the parcel address as the city lists it. Second, call or visit the Tax Collector and ask for the payoff through a specific closing date, because interest keeps adding up at the 1.5% monthly rate once a bill is late. Third, pass the figure to your title company and ask them to confirm it against their own search. If your closing slips by a few weeks, the number can change, so ask for an updated figure rather than assuming the first one still holds.

Write down who you spoke with and the date, and keep the figure with your closing papers. If you rent the house out, tell the tenants why a title company may contact them, so a request for access or information does not come as a surprise.

sections.h2: Selling a Hartford house with back taxes
sections.html:
You can. The unpaid tax is normally taken from your proceeds at closing, so it does not have to be paid up front. In order: request the payoff, check for a lien, give the numbers to the title company, and choose a closing date once those answers are in hand.

Many Hartford sellers hold inherited houses, vacant houses or multi-family buildings with tenants in place, and each of those adds a step. An estate needs someone authorized to sign. An occupied building needs a plan for access before anyone can see it. Because buyers here often care more about what condition the building is in than which street it is on, a house needing work can be easier to sell as-is than to repair and list.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Hartford houses as-is, including those with back taxes, and the title company settles what is owed from the proceeds.

faqs.q: When are Hartford property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is due July 1 and January 1. The last days to pay are August 1 and February 1, moved to Monday when they fall on a weekend.

faqs.q: What interest does Hartford charge on late real estate tax?
faqs.a: Late balances accrue interest at 1.5% per month, which the city states as 18% per year.

faqs.q: Is there a different payment plan for elderly Hartford owners?
faqs.a: Yes, for approved applications only. It uses four installments, due July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hartford house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing normally pays the tax out of your proceeds, so you need not pay it first. Ask the tax office for the payoff and have your title company confirm the figure.

faqs.q: Who files the Connecticut conveyance tax return?
faqs.a: The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded.
